Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: As she sat in her small apartment, surrounded by photographs of her late husband and their life together, 58-year-old Rachel couldn't help but feel a sense of dread wash over her. It had been two years since the accident that took his life, but for Rachel, time seemed to have stood still. She was certain that on the anniversary of that fateful day, she would be transported back to the moment when everything changed. Rachel's husband had been driving home from work when another car ran a red light and slammed into his vehicle. The sound of screeching tires and crunching metal still echoed in her mind, and the smell of smoke and gasoline often wafted up unexpectedly, carrying with it the memories she tried to keep at bay. She remembered the feeling of panic that gripped her as she rushed to the hospital, only to be met with the devastating news that he didn't survive. In the days and weeks that followed, Rachel found herself on high alert, constantly scanning her surroundings for potential threats. The sound of an ambulance siren in the distance would send her heart racing, and the sight of a car accident on the news would leave her shaken. She began to avoid driving altogether, fearing that she might be the next victim. Her friends and family tried to reassure her, but Rachel couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. As time went by, Rachel's sleep patterns became increasingly disrupted. She would lie awake at night, replaying the events of that terrible day in her mind, trying to make sense of it all. Her mind racing with worst-case scenarios, she found herself getting out of bed multiple times a night to check that the doors and windows were locked, just to be sure. But it wasn't just the memories of that day that haunted Rachel; it was also the fragments that refused to coalesce into a coherent narrative. When she tried to deliberately recall the events surrounding her husband's accident, she found herself drawing a blank. It was as if her mind had put up a barrier, shielding her from the full force of the trauma. And yet, without warning, something in her surroundings would trigger the memory, and Rachel would be instantly transported back to that moment. A glimpse of a car with a dented bumper, the sound of screeching tires on the road outside – anything could send her spiraling into a vortex of fear and anxiety. As the months went by, Rachel became increasingly isolated. She stopped leaving the house, afraid of what might happen if she ventured out. Her relationships began to fray, as friends and family grew tired of her constant avoidance and hypervigilance. And yet, for Rachel, it felt like the only way to stay safe. As she sat in her apartment, surrounded by the memories of a life that no longer was, Rachel knew she needed help. She couldn't keep living in this state of constant fear, always looking over her shoulder, waiting for the other shoe to drop. With a sense of trepidation, she picked up the phone and dialed the number of a therapist who specialized in trauma, hoping against hope that someone could finally help her find a way out of this prison of her own making. For Rachel, seeking help was both a necessary step towards healing and a terrifying prospect. What if she wasn't strong enough to face her demons? What if she got stuck forever in this limbo of grief and fear? But as she looked around her apartment, at the photographs and mementos that told the story of a life cut short, Rachel knew she had no choice but to try.
